title: Malloy Semantic Layer: What It Is & How To Use It In 2026
summary: Malloy is the semantic layer we recommend for AI analytics: open source, joins and measures defined once, queries compiled to SQL. Why, how, and its limits.
body_markdown:
**Malloy is the semantic layer we recommend for AI analytics: an open-source (MIT) language for semantic modeling and querying that compiles to SQL.** It was started at Google Cloud by Lloyd Tabb, the Looker co-founder who designed LookML, and as of October 2026 it runs on BigQuery, Snowflake, PostgreSQL, DuckDB, MotherDuck, MySQL, Trino, Presto and Databricks. As a semantic layer for AI agents it does four things unusually well: an agent asks for a measure by name instead of re-deriving its formula, aggregates stay correct across joins, every query is checked against the model before any SQL runs, and a restricted mode keeps LLM-written queries inside the model. The costs are real too: Malloy is still labelled experimental, its ecosystem is small, and language models know SQL far better than they know Malloy.


The Malloy code below compiles and runs as written (` @malloydata/malloy` 0.0.436 on DuckDB, October 2026), and the SQL shown is the compiler's actual output.


## What Malloy is


The project describes Malloy as “a semantic modeling and query language built on top of SQL.” You define a *source* once (a table plus its joins, dimensions, measures and saved views) and write short queries against it; the compiler turns each into SQL that runs where your data lives. The first GitHub commit came in August 2021, after Google bought Looker ([BigDATAwire](https://www.bigdatawire.com/2022/05/03/looker-founder-helps-create-new-data-exploration-language-malloy) ). It keeps LookML’s central idea (put joins and measures in a model so nobody re-derives them) and adds a query language of its own.


- **Maturity:** the[malloydata/malloy](https://github.com/malloydata/malloy) README no longer says “experimental”, but the[malloydata GitHub organization](https://github.com/malloydata) still describes Malloy as “an experimental language for describing data relationships and transformations”. Packages are versioned 0.0.x and ship every few weeks ([v0.0.436](https://github.com/malloydata/malloy/releases) on October 26, 2026), and the[4.0 revision](https://lloydtabb.substack.com/p/announcing-malloy-40) in October 2023 turned code written in the older syntax from warnings into errors.
- **Commercial backing:**[Publisher](https://github.com/malloydata/publisher) , the open-source model server, is “created and maintained by Credible”, a startup building a governed context engine for AI on top of Malloy, which[announced a $10 million seed round](https://pulse2.com/credible-data-raises-10-million-seed-round-to-bring-governed-business-context-to-enterprise-ai/) in July 2026.
- **Learning material:** the[official documentation](https://docs.malloydata.dev/documentation/) and the[malloy-samples](https://github.com/malloydata/malloy-samples) repo (e-commerce, flights, IMDb, GA4 and more).


## Core concepts in one model


Here is a small, complete` .malloy` file: three tables, two joins, a few dimensions and measures, and one saved view.


```text
// index.malloy: a small e-commerce model
source: users is duckdb.table('users') extend {
primary_key: id
}


source: products is duckdb.table('products') extend {
primary_key: id
}


source: order_items is duckdb.table('order_items') extend {
primary_key: id


join_one: users with user_id
join_one: products with product_id


dimension:
order_month is created_at.month
#" An item that was neither cancelled nor returned
is_valid is status != 'Cancelled' & 'Returned'


measure:
#" Net revenue: sale price of valid items
revenue is sale_price.sum() { where: is_valid }
#" Distinct orders with at least one valid item
order_count is count(order_id) { where: is_valid }
#" Revenue per order
average_order_value is revenue / order_count
#" Distinct customers with a valid order
customer_count is count(user_id) { where: is_valid }
#" Cost of goods sold: product cost once per item sold
cogs is source.sum(products.cost) { where: is_valid }
gross_margin is revenue - cogs


view: revenue_by_month is {
group_by: order_month
aggregate: revenue, order_count
order_by: order_month
}
}
```


### Sources and joins


A` source` is a table (or a query) extended with modeling.` primary_key` says what makes a row unique, and` join_one: users with user_id` joins on that key: each order item has one user.` join_many` declares the other direction and` join_cross` a cross product. Joins are left outer by default, and Malloy keeps them as a graph rather than one wide table; the[join documentation](https://docs.malloydata.dev/documentation/language/join) says aggregates navigate that graph “so they are always computed correctly regardless of join pattern, avoiding the fan and chasm traps.”


### Dimensions and measures


A` dimension` is a per-row value you group or filter by; a` measure` is an aggregate. Measures build on each other (` average_order_value is revenue / order_count` ) and can carry their own filters (` { where: is_valid }` ). Two details trip up people coming from SQL:` count(order_id)` is a distinct count, and` status != 'Cancelled' & 'Returned'` means “neither cancelled nor returned”. The` #"` lines are[description annotations](https://docs.malloydata.dev/documentation/language/tags) , which an agent reads to tell two similar measures apart, so write them.


### Views and refinements


A` view` is a saved query on a source. Run it as it is, or refine it with` +` to add a filter or a grouping without copying it:


```text
run: order_items -> revenue_by_month


run: order_items -> revenue_by_month + { where: users.country = 'Germany' }
```


The first query compiles to this DuckDB SQL. The` revenue` and` order_count` definitions, including the cancelled and returned rule, arrive in the SQL without the query mentioning them:


```text
SELECT
DATE_TRUNC('month', base."created_at") as "order_month",
COALESCE(SUM(CASE WHEN ((COALESCE(base."status"!='Cancelled',true)) and (COALESCE(base."status"!='Returned',true))) THEN base."sale_price" END),0) as "revenue",
count(distinct CASE WHEN ((COALESCE(base."status"!='Cancelled',true)) and (COALESCE(base."status"!='Returned',true))) THEN base."order_id" END) as "order_count"
FROM order_items as base
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1 ASC NULLS LAST
```


Views can also be chained into multi-stage pipelines with` ->` , each stage becoming a CTE, and can use` calculate:` for window functions such as` rank()` ([views documentation](https://docs.malloydata.dev/documentation/language/views) ).


### Nested queries


Nesting returns a summary row per group with a subtable inside each row, which has no single-clause SQL equivalent. This query returns each country’s 2026 revenue and customers plus its two best sellers:


```text
run: order_items -> {
where: created_at ? @2026
group_by: users.country
aggregate: revenue, customer_count
nest: top_products is {
group_by: products.name
aggregate: revenue
limit: 2
}
}
```


The SQL Malloy generated on DuckDB:


```text
WITH __stage0 AS (
SELECT
group_set,
users_0."country" as "country__0",
CASE WHEN group_set=0 THEN
COALESCE(SUM(CASE WHEN ((COALESCE(base."status"!='Cancelled',true)) and (COALESCE(base."status"!='Returned',true))) THEN base."sale_price" END),0)
END as "revenue__0",
CASE WHEN group_set=0 THEN
count(distinct CASE WHEN ((COALESCE(base."status"!='Cancelled',true)) and (COALESCE(base."status"!='Returned',true))) THEN base."user_id" END)
END as "customer_count__0",
CASE WHEN group_set=1 THEN
products_0."name"
END as "name__1",
CASE WHEN group_set=1 THEN
END as "revenue__1"
FROM order_items as base
LEFT JOIN users AS users_0
ON users_0."id"=base."user_id"
LEFT JOIN products AS products_0
ON products_0."id"=base."product_id"
CROSS JOIN (SELECT UNNEST(GENERATE_SERIES(0,1,1)) as group_set  ) as group_set
WHERE (base."created_at">=TIMESTAMP '2026-01-01 00:00:00') and (base."created_at"<TIMESTAMP '2027-01-01 00:00:00')
GROUP BY 1,2,5
)
, __stage1 AS (
SELECT
*,
CASE WHEN GROUP_SET=1 THEN
ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY CAST("country__0" as VARCHAR), group_set ORDER BY  "revenue__1" desc) END  as __row_number__1
FROM __stage0
)
, __stage2 AS (
SELECT * FROM __stage1
WHERE  NOT ((GROUP_SET = 1 AND __row_number__1 > 2))
)
SELECT
"country__0" as "country",
MAX(CASE WHEN group_set=0 THEN "revenue__0" END) as "revenue",
MAX(CASE WHEN group_set=0 THEN "customer_count__0" END) as "customer_count",
COALESCE(LIST({
"name": "name__1",
"revenue": "revenue__1"}  ORDER BY  "revenue__1" DESC NULLS LAST) FILTER (WHERE group_set=1),[]) as "top_products"
FROM __stage2
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 2 desc NULLS LAST
```


That is a cross join against a group-set series, a window function and a list aggregate. Asking a model to hand-write that for every “top N within each group” question invites subtle bugs; in Malloy it is one` nest:` , and nests can go several levels deep ([nesting documentation](https://docs.malloydata.dev/documentation/language/nesting) ).


### How Malloy compiles to SQL across dialects


Each` connection.table()` names a connection, and the compiler emits SQL in its dialect: moving the model from DuckDB to BigQuery means changing` duckdb.table('order_items')` to something like` bigquery.table('my-project.shop.order_items')` , with measures, views and queries unchanged. SQL Server, Oracle and ClickHouse are not among the engines the[README](https://github.com/malloydata/malloy) lists. DuckDB is the easiest start (a model over Parquet runs on a laptop); on BigQuery, see our[BigQuery MCP guide](https://www.getdot.ai/blog/bigquery-mcp-server) .


## Why we recommend Malloy for AI agents


An agent answering data questions re-derives a metric slightly differently each time, double-counts across a join, references a column that does not exist, or wanders into tables nobody vetted. Malloy has a specific answer to each, below. With what the sections above showed (one MIT project for model and queries, nine SQL engines, a nest for “top N in each group”), that is why we recommend it.


### Measures are names, not formulas


With raw SQL, every question about revenue makes the model rewrite revenue: which statuses to exclude, which column, which grain. With Malloy the agent writes` aggregate: revenue` and the compiler inlines the one definition, as the SQL above shows. The definition can still be wrong, but it is wrong in one place, a plain-text file in Git where a fix is a reviewable diff that corrects every later answer.


### Aggregates stay correct across joins


Fan-out is the classic silent error in model-written SQL. Malloy makes the grain of every aggregate explicit. In the model above,` cogs is source.sum(products.cost)` adds a product’s cost once per item sold;` products.cost.sum()` adds each product’s cost once, full stop:


```text
run: order_items -> {
aggregate:
cogs
distinct_product_cost is products.cost.sum() { where: is_valid }
}
```


On a nine-row test dataset built for this post, where several items share a product,` cogs` returns 194 and` distinct_product_cost` returns 119. Both are legitimate questions; if an agent writes the ambiguous` sum(products.cost)` , the compiler warns:


```text
Join path is required for this calculation; use `products.cost.sum()` or `source.sum(products.cost)` to get a result weighted with respect to `source`
```


An agent can apply that fix on its next turn. Per the[aggregate locality rules](https://docs.malloydata.dev/documentation/language/aggregates) ,` sum` and` avg` need an explicit locality when they reach through a join;` count` ,` min` and` max` do not.


### The compiler catches mistakes before the warehouse does


Every Malloy query is compiled against the model first. Ask for a field that does not exist:


```text
run: order_items -> {
group_by: users.region
aggregate: revenue
}
```


and you get` 'region' is not defined` (error code` field-not-found` ) before a single byte is scanned. For an agent that is a cheap, exact feedback loop: compile, read the error, fix, compile again.


### A restricted mode for LLM-written queries


Malloy’s runtime (as of 0.0.436) has a` loadRestrictedQuery` method whose[doc comment](https://github.com/malloydata/malloy/blob/main/packages/malloy/src/api/foundation/runtime.ts) says it is for a query “whose text comes from an untrusted source”, naming “an MCP client, an LLM-authored query” among the examples. In restricted mode the compiler rejects` import` statements, raw` connection.table()` and` connection.sql()` sources and raw SQL functions (error` restricted-construct-forbidden` ), while every source, measure and view in the model stays available. That turns “only use the semantic layer” from a prompt instruction into a compiler rule.


## Where Malloy falls short


**Models know SQL much better than Malloy.** MotherDuck tested this directly. In its[agentic-malloy experiment](https://github.com/motherduckdb/labs/tree/main/projects/agentic-malloy) on Adyen’s DABstep benchmark, an agent (Sonnet authoring, Opus as fixer) built a Malloy model from a 26-question training set and then answered about 419 held-out questions through it. Malloy scored 382 of 419 (91.2%); the Markdown plus SQL baseline scored 418 of 419 (99.8%), and Malloy used about 2.5 times the prompt tokens. The write-up calls the hypothesis “not supported”, says the layer was “mostly bypassed”, and found the model-written Malloy itself accurate ([MotherDuck’s discussion](https://motherduck.com/blog/AI-writes-the-semantic-layer/) ).


That matches our own result: we took Dot[from 10% to 90%](https://www.getdot.ai/blog/from-10-to-90-percent-on-adyens-dabstep) on a DABstep slice without a semantic layer. DABstep is multi-step analysis over one payments dataset, which in my read rewards flexible SQL more than shared definitions, so many people asking about the same few dozen metrics is a different workload. Still, Malloy does not make an agent more accurate on its own.


**A young project.** 0.0.x versions and an “experimental” label mean you pin versions, keep queries under test and expect the occasional breaking change.


**A small ecosystem.** Malloy’s own tools cover modeling (VS Code extension), queries (CLI, npm), simple dashboards (Composer) and serving (Publisher, Malloyyo); for business users you build or buy the front end.


**The model has to tell the truth about keys.** Malloy’s join math depends on primary keys and on` join_one` really being one-to-one; its[troubleshooting guide](https://docs.malloydata.dev/documentation/user_guides/troubleshooting) warns that when it is not, results inflate silently. The compiler checks names and types, not your data.


**It solves computation, not orientation.** It makes “compute net revenue” deterministic but doesn’t decide which of your revenue numbers someone meant; see[the semantic layer solves the wrong half](https://www.getdot.ai/blog/the-semantic-layer-solves-the-wrong-half) and[what a semantic layer is](https://www.getdot.ai/blog/semantic-layer) .


## Malloy and MCP: Publisher and Malloyyo


Two open-source, MIT-licensed projects put a Malloy model in front of Claude, Cursor or an agent you build.


### Publisher


[Publisher](https://github.com/malloydata/publisher) , created and maintained by Credible, loads Malloy packages and serves them through a web UI, a REST API and MCP. It starts with three bundled DuckDB example packages and no credentials, and Claude Code can register its MCP endpoint with one command:


```text
npx @malloy-publisher/server@latest --port 4000


# in a second terminal: register the MCP endpoint with Claude Code
claude mcp add --transport http malloy http://127.0.0.1:4040/mcp -s user
```


Cursor, VS Code, Codex and Claude Desktop use the same endpoint. Its tools include` get_context` (discover sources, views and fields),` execute_query` ,` search_database_schema` ,` compile_model` and` reload_package` . Access control is written into the model: givens for runtime parameters,` #(access_filter)` for row-level access and` #(authorize)` to gate a whole source.


The README says the server, MCP and REST alike, is “stateless and unauthenticated” and can read any data your models connect to. It recommends binding to loopback (` --host 127.0.0.1` ) for local use and an authenticating gateway before exposing it more widely: the access annotations decide what a caller may see, but something else has to establish who the caller is.


### Malloyyo


[Malloyyo](https://github.com/malloydata/malloyyo) , in the malloydata organization, describes itself as a way to “serve any AI a Malloy semantic model over MCP”: set up a repo, have Claude build the model, publish it to a Malloyyo server, then ask questions or build dashboards in Claude or on the web. “The AI can only query what the model exposes,” and datasets are granted to roles. DuckDB is built in; BigQuery, Snowflake, MotherDuck, Databricks and Postgres are listed too.


```text
npm install -g @malloydata/malloyyo
cd my-model-repo
malloyyo init       # sets the repo up for Claude
claude              # "connect to my warehouse and build a Malloy model from these dbt sources"
malloyyo publish    # push it to your Malloyyo server
```


It calls itself “a small tool”, so treat it as early software.


## Malloy vs LookML


Same designer, same core idea, different scope.
